newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: European summit to discuss arms pact, not NATO.
newsitem.headline: European summit to discuss arms pact, not NATO.

text.p: Western nations intend to focus on conventional arms cuts at a European security summit next week and steer clear of Russian concerns over NATO expansion, diplomats said on Saturday.

Leaders of the 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), meeting in Lisbon on Monday and Tuesday, are expected to authorise a fresh round of negotiations in Vienna next year on reducing military equipment, such as tanks, aircraft and armoured vehicles.

The talks would seek to adapt the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty signed in 1990 between NATO and the former Warsaw Pact and extend it to newly-independent states, in particular the former Soviet republics.

"We recognise that the treaty as it stands is an important cornerstone of European security, but it no longer corresponds to the state of play," a senior member of the U.S. delegation to the Lisbon summit said.
"The United States is very much behind the modernisation negotiations," he added.
Moscow has been pressing for changes to the CFE treaty so that it no longer reflects the old Cold War East-West divide, arguing that Russia now faces superior NATO forces.

Diplomatic sources said it was hoped the go-ahead for what would largely be a re-negotiation of the CFE pact would be enough to defuse any potential friction at the summit over NATO's expansion into central and eastern Europe.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Friday reiterated Moscow's opposition to new members, which were once part of the Soviet bloc, joining NATO.
The 16-nation Western alliance is expected to announce next year which countries can join, with Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic seen as the most likely candidates.

"Russia's stance on NATO expansion remains unchanged, that is, negative," a Kremlin spokesman quoted Yeltsin as saying. "Whether it is intended or not, NATO expansion will lead to new divisions in Europe."
Moscow's vision of a future European security model would be to create a greater role for the OSCE as a counterbalance to NATO. But the likelihood of such an idea being adopted in Lisbon is slim.

The United States and other NATO members prefer to see the OSCE working more with organisations such as the European Union and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) to anchor security in Europe in the economic and human rights as well as military spheres.
Any proposal for the OSCE to have a superior role to NATO would be a non-starter.

One possible source of friction at the summit may come from Azerbaijan, which is pressing for its integrity as a sovereign state to be recognised, one European diplomatic source said. Armenia wants the enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh to be given self-determination.

The last OSCE summit in Budapest in 1994 agreed to send a peacekeeping force to Nagorno-Karabakh, where Azerbaijanis and ethnic Armenians have fought to a stalemate, leaving the Armenians in control. But peace talks between Azerbaijan and Armenia have made little progress.
OSCE decision-making is based on consensus and Azerbaijan could hold up a summit final document, or veto it, if it failed to get its way. REUTER
